---
title: "Methods"
---

Implementation notes for the parts of the analysis that are easy to misread from the
code alone. The manuscript methods section is the authoritative description.

## Model

One XGBoost regressor per site, target `NEP_ZSCORE`, predictors `TA_ZSCORE`,
`SWIN_ZSCORE`, `VPD_ZSCORE`, `SWC_ZSCORE`. Settings live in `src/models.py`.

## Flux targets

The published analysis explains `NEP_ZSCORE`. The same models and the same settings
also run for three other targets, which support the decomposition arguments in the
revision rather than the headline result. All four use the full 208 sites.

| Target | Source variable | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `NEP_ZSCORE` | `NEE_VUT_50`, sign flipped | Measured, quality flag 0 only |
| `GPP_ZSCORE` | `GPP_NT_VUT_50` | Partitioning product |
| `RECO_ZSCORE` | `RECO_NT_VUT_50` | Partitioning product |
| `ET_ZSCORE` | derived from `LE_F_MDS` | Includes gap-filled values |

How well the four targets fit, measured as the out-of-sample global R2 per site and
summarised over the 208 sites:

| Target | Mean | Median | p10 | p90 | Min | Max | Sites below 0.40 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| NEP | 0.622 | 0.643 | 0.43 | 0.77 | 0.232 | 0.855 | 17 |
| GPP | 0.652 | 0.670 | 0.49 | 0.78 | 0.245 | 0.951 | 12 |
| RECO | 0.579 | 0.584 | 0.34 | 0.77 | 0.111 | 0.980 | 27 |
| ET | 0.652 | 0.668 | 0.52 | 0.78 | 0.273 | 0.872 | 6 |

GPP fits better than NEP, which is expected, because NEP is the difference between two
larger fluxes and carries the noise of both. ET fits about as well as GPP on average and
is the most consistent of the four, with the highest p10 and only 6 sites below 0.40.
Part of that consistency comes from the target itself rather than from the model, since
ET is derived from gap-filled latent heat flux (see below).

Two caveats matter when reading GPP or RECO results.

`RECO_NT_VUT_50` comes from a temperature response fitted to night-time NEE and
extrapolated into the day, and GPP is that RECO minus NEE. Both are therefore model
products, and part of any temperature signal in their attribution belongs to the
partitioning model rather than to the ecosystem. The effect is not uniform: RECO fits
worse than NEP on average (mean global R2 0.579 against 0.622) but spans a much wider
range, 0.111 to 0.980, with 27 sites below 0.40 and 2 above 0.90. So the partitioning
shows through at a few sites, not everywhere. Use the decomposition to say which
component drives a change in NEP, not to quantify the temperature sensitivity of RECO.

`ET_ZSCORE` is derived from latent heat flux. The quality filter on `LE` is disabled
in `src/files.py`, because the FLUXNET flag marks every LE record as gap-filled, so ET
is not the quality-flag-0 product that NEP is.
Fixed across SHAP, ALE and tuning:

```python
tree_method='hist'
subsample=0.8
colsample_bytree=0.8
reg_lambda=1.0
reg_alpha=0.1
gamma=0.2
min_child_weight=5
early_stopping_rounds=100
```

### Cross-validation

Two strategies, set by `CV_STRATEGY` in script `31`.

`random`, the default and the one behind the published results, is a shuffled 5-fold
split of the complete rows. It matches the task: a gap is predicted from driver values at
its own timestamp, and gaps sit between observed records.

`blocked` leaves one calendar year out at a time. Neighbouring half-hours are correlated,
so a shuffled split can put a record and its neighbour on opposite sides and flatter the
score. A year-wise split removes that. Sites with a single year are skipped.

Measured over 206 sites: mean out-of-sample R2 falls from 0.622 to 0.510 and RMSE rises
from 0.606 to 0.691, with a lower score at every site. The attribution barely moves. At
the compound-extreme stage the VPD contribution is -0.4286 under random and -0.4287 under
blocked, while the soil water contribution weakens from -0.0852 to -0.0638.

Read them as answers to different questions. The random split says how well the model
fills gaps inside the observed period, the blocked split says whether it transfers to an
unseen year.

### Predictor sets

`FEATURE_SET` in script `31` selects the drivers. `full` is the submitted set of TA, SW,
VPD and SM. `no_vpd` drops VPD and keeps TA, `no_ta` does the reverse. Both alternatives
were run over all 208 sites.

| set | mean R2 | median R2 |
|---|---|---|
| full | 0.622 | 0.643 |
| no VPD | 0.580 | 0.597 |
| no TA | 0.590 | 0.608 |

Dropping either variable lowers the score at 205 of the 208 sites, so neither is
redundant. Dropping TA costs less than dropping VPD.

Each variable takes over part of the other's role when removed. The median mean absolute
SHAP for TA goes from 0.106 to 0.194 without VPD, and VPD goes from 0.179 to 0.216
without TA. Read the attributions in the full model as conditional on the other variable
being present.

The `no_ta` run is carried through the aggregation as well, so the threshold can be
re-estimated from models that never saw temperature. It comes out at 1.28 kPa, with a
prediction band of 1.19 to 1.37 over the same 208 sites, against the published 1.26. That is
one of the rows of Table 1. Air temperature still bins the grid there, as it does in every
other row: the `no_ta` files keep the `TA_ZSCORE` data column and only lack
`TA_ZSCORE_SHAPVALS`, so the estimator is unchanged and only the model behind the SHAP values
differs.

A third alternative, TA with a different humidity variable, is not available. No site in
the analysis records RH, and humidity variables that could be derived from these data are
exact functions of TA and VPD.

Searched during tuning:

```python
n_estimators  = [2000, 2500, 3000, 3500, 4000]
max_depth     = [4, 5, 6, 7, 8]
learning_rate = [0.01, 0.03, 0.05, 0.07, 0.1]
```

The grid is 125 combinations; with 5-fold cross-validation that is 625 fits per site,
which is why tuning is a separate mode rather than part of every run. The
regularisation parameters are held fixed so tuned and untuned runs stay comparable.

## SHAP

`TreeExplainer` with `feature_perturbation="tree_path_dependent"`. TA and VPD are
strongly dependent, and breaking that dependence would ask the model about combinations
of temperature and humidity that never occur. The tree-path-dependent variant keeps the
observed joint distribution.

What this gives is a conditional attribution: how the fitted model distributes its
prediction among correlated predictors. It is not a separation of physiological causes.

SHAP values are out-of-sample. Each fold explains only the 20 % that its model never
trained on.

## ALE

`PyALE.ale`, 100 grid points per feature, one model per site fitted on 85 % of the
records with 15 % held back for early stopping, then applied to all records of that
site. Note this is a separate fit from the cross-validated models behind the SHAP
values, so the two are not the same trees.

ALE and SHAP interrogate the same fitted models on the same observations, so agreement
between them says the reading is robust to the interpretation method. It is not
independent validation of the underlying physiology.

## Soil water depth {#soil-water-depth}

The submitted analysis uses `SWC_F_MDS_1`, the shallowest gap-filled soil water layer,
because it is the one nearly every site records. Shallow soil dries faster than the soil
trees actually draw from, which raises the question of whether atmospheric demand only
looks dominant because the soil water proxy is too shallow.

`21_prepare_input_data.py` can therefore run on the deepest layer instead:

```python
SWC_LAYER = "shallow"   # SWC_F_MDS_1
SWC_LAYER = "deepest"   # deepest usable layer per site
```

The rule is in `src/common.py::deepest_swc_per_site()`. For each site, take the deepest
layer that still holds at least 90 % of layer 1's records within the four peak months.
If no deeper layer clears that bar, the site keeps layer 1.

The coverage floor is doing real work. Deeper sensors are often gappier, and a gappier
predictor means fewer complete records, so a site could differ between the two runs
because its sample shrank rather than because its soil water came from further down.
Without the floor, 18 sites would have run on a much sparser layer. With it, no site
keeps less than 90.6 % of its shallow records, and the median is 100 %.

Under that rule 128 of 208 sites move to a deeper layer, spread across layers 2 to 9.
The remaining 80 have no deeper layer, or only layers too sparse to use, and their
results are unchanged by construction.

Depths in centimetres cannot be recovered. Only three sites carry `GRP_SWC` depth
metadata in the AmeriFlux BIF, so this is the deepest available layer, never the root
zone at a stated depth.

### What a deep run contains

A deep run keeps all 208 sites. The 128 that have a usable deeper layer move to it, and
the other 80 stay on layer 1, because dropping them would change the site set as well as
the depth. So a deep-run figure shows the deepest available layer per site, not deep soil
water everywhere, and roughly two fifths of the sites contribute exactly what they
contribute to the shallow run. Their SHAP values come back bit-identical.

That damps the difference between the two runs. To see the effect of depth on its own,
most scripts from 41 onwards take a second switch:

```python
SITE_SUBSET = ""              # every site
SITE_SUBSET = "deeper-only"   # the 128 sites below layer 1
```

Run it against both variants and the result is a matched pair: the same 128 sites, the
same records, differing only in sensor depth. Output goes to its own folder, so the
mixed run and the submitted run stay where they are.

The 128 are the 127 sites the depth rule moves, plus CA-Obs, which already used layer 2
in the submitted analysis because layer 1 was missing there.

### What the comparison showed

Soil water gains importance and VPD loses some, but the ordering does not change. Across all 208 sites the stage 8 ratio of VPD to soil water
attribution goes from 5.03 to 4.86. Restricted to the 128 sites that actually moved, it
goes from 4.22 to 4.00. Site-level importance shifts more where the layer swap goes
deeper, from no change at layer 2 to roughly a quarter of the ratio at layers 7 to 9.

Evergreen broadleaf sites are the weak spot: only 10 of 30 have a usable deeper layer,
and those are the arid and seasonally dry forests where the question bites hardest.

## Stress stages

Nine subsets of the half-hourly records, defined on z-scores in `src/stages.py`. The
cut-offs are standard-normal equivalents: 0.319 bounds the middle 25 %, 0.714 the next
band, and 1.282 the upper or lower 10 %.

| Stage | Condition |
|-------|-----------|
| 0 | all data, unrestricted |
| 1 | normal: TA, VPD and SWC all within the middle 25 % |
| 2 | warm, soil moisture normal, no extreme VPD |
| 3 | warm and dry soil, no extreme VPD |
| 4 | hot, drier soil, no extreme VPD |
| 5 | hot, very dry soil, no extreme VPD |
| 6 | extremely hot, very dry soil, no extreme VPD |
| 7 | extremely hot, extremely dry soil, no extreme VPD |
| 8 | compound extreme: extremely hot, extremely dry soil and extremely dry air |

Stages 2 to 7 cap VPD at the 90th percentile so they do not overlap with the compound
extreme in stage 8.

Script `45` reports the driver distributions inside each stage, in standardized and in
measured units, globally and per forest type. Median across sites of the site median:

| stage | TA sigma | VPD sigma | SM sigma | SW sigma | TA degC | VPD hPa | SW W/m2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 all data | 0.05 | -0.12 | -0.11 | 0.01 | 20.8 | 9.8 | 492 |
| 1 normal | 0.03 | -0.02 | -0.02 | 0.34 | 20.8 | 10.5 | 567 |
| 4 hot and dry | 0.93 | 0.67 | -0.51 | 0.49 | 25.3 | 14.7 | 618 |
| 8 compound | 1.69 | 2.15 | -1.54 | 0.65 | 28.9 | 23.4 | 634 |

No stage definition constrains shortwave radiation, but it rises across the stages
anyway, from 0.01 to 0.65 sigma, or 492 to 634 W/m2, because hot dry days are sunny days.
SW is the strongest positive contributor in the model, so the step from stage 1 to stage
8 changes light as well as heat and dryness.

Stage 1 already sits at 0.34 sigma of SW. The peak-season and daytime filters select
bright records, so "normal conditions" means normal in heat and dryness, not in light.
Stages 6 and 7 share a VPD of about 0.98 sigma and differ only in soil moisture.

::: {.callout-note}
The stages are not a balanced factorial design. VPD varies within stages where soil
moisture is held near baseline, and there is no mirrored stage where soil moisture
varies while VPD is held near baseline.
:::

### Is the threshold an artefact of standardization?

A site with a narrow VPD range reaches +3 sigma at a modest absolute VPD, so a threshold
in sigma could in principle come from the standardization rather than from a limit on the
plant. Script `82` tests this.

The direct test is not possible here. It would need sites whose VPD never exceeds about
1.25 kPa, and no site in the analysis stays that low. The lowest site maximum is 1.69 kPa
and the median is 3.86 kPa. Sites are therefore split into quartiles of their own maximum
VPD.

| quartile | n | median max VPD | threshold sigma | threshold kPa | sites with a crossing |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| lowest | 52 | 2.90 | 0.25 | 1.00 | 52 |
| Q2 | 52 | 3.60 | 0.29 | 1.15 | 52 |
| Q3 | 51 | 4.38 | 0.16 | 1.32 | 51 |
| highest | 52 | 5.69 | 0.04 | 1.41 | 52 |

Every site in every quartile produces a zero crossing, so the nonlinear response is not
limited to sites that reach high absolute VPD.

The absolute threshold is not constant. It rises with the site's VPD range, Spearman rho
+0.47. From the lowest to the highest quartile the range grows 96 per cent while the
threshold grows 41 per cent. Proportional growth would point to the standardization,
no growth to a fixed physical limit, and the data sit between the two.

The spread across VPD quartiles, 1.00 to 1.41 kPa, is wider than the spread across forest
types, 1.22 to 1.32 kPa.

### Does the network composition matter?

Europe and North America hold 74 per cent of the sites, 56 and 98 of 208. Script `83`
drops each region and recomputes, using the country prefix of the site code.

| set | sites | threshold kPa | VPD/SM ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| all sites | 207 | 1.19 | 5.03 |
| minus Europe | 151 | 1.24 | 5.86 |
| minus North America | 109 | 1.11 | 5.94 |
| minus both | 53 | 1.12 | 60.56 |

The threshold moves by at most 0.08 kPa, even with three quarters of the network removed.

The ratio does not behave. Outside Europe and North America it reads 60.6, because the
mean soil water contribution there is -0.0049, near zero, and 24 of those 44 sites have a
positive contribution. A ratio whose denominator straddles zero is not a usable quantity.

Note that 1.19 kPa is the median of the per-site thresholds, while the 1.26 kPa quoted
earlier is the crossing of the aggregated curve. Two different quantities.

### Does record length matter?

Fifteen sites keep fewer than three years, and two keep one year, although a three-year
minimum is stated. The minimum is applied before the QC, daytime, peak-month and
balancing filters, which then cut into the record. Script `84` checks whether those sites
change anything.

| minimum years | sites | records kept | threshold kPa |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1, all sites | 207 | 100.0 % | 1.19 |
| 3 | 192 | 98.7 % | 1.19 |
| 5 | 144 | 88.9 % | 1.16 |
| 10 | 72 | 63.8 % | 1.10 |

Enforcing the stated three-year minimum drops 15 sites and 1.3 per cent of the records,
and leaves the threshold unchanged. Requiring ten years discards two thirds of the sites
and moves it to 1.10 kPa.

## Aggregation across sites

Every site contributes one curve or one binned grid, regardless of how many records it
has. Aggregated bins are kept only where at least half of the sites have data, which
controls how sparsely a bin is covered across the network.

Site-level means are combined with the law of total variance in `src/stages.py`, so the
reported spread carries both the within-site variance and the variance between site
means. Bars in the stage figures use the standard error of the site means.

## Threshold detection

Two independent routes to the VPD value where the effect on NEP turns negative.

From SHAP (script `54`): bin the aggregated SHAP values against VPD, fit a fourth-order
polynomial, take the zero crossing.

From ALE (script `46`): fit a fourth-order polynomial to each site's ALE curve first,
then average the fitted curves. The threshold is the mean of the zero crossings of the
individual site curves, not the crossing of the averaged curve. Reported alongside it are
the number of sites that cross and a 95 % interval on that mean, from the t distribution.
The crossing of the pooled curve is a different number, 0.107 against 0.181 sigma, and it
is written out beside the mean so the two cannot be confused.

Smoothing before averaging keeps the shape of individual curves from cancelling out.
Both values are zero crossings of a model attribution, not measured physiological
breakpoints.

### From sigma to kPa

Each site standardizes VPD against its own mean and standard deviation, so a threshold
in sigma is a different absolute VPD at every site. Script `54` converts it, in the same
script that fits the curve, and writes the supplementary table of coefficients:

1. per site, `VPD_abs = site mean VPD + z * site SD`, both in hPa over the records the
   models saw, then divided by 10 for kPa
2. sites averaged with equal weight, the same one vote per site used elsewhere, and the
   biome value is the mean over that biome's sites
3. the interval bounds come from putting the sigma interval through the same conversion,
   not from a separate calculation
4. CD-Ygb is converted, because it records VPD in Pa where every other site uses hPa.
   The factor is exactly 100. Feeding the raw values in without converting moves the
   global threshold from 1.26 to 2.19 kPa, so the site must never be used unconverted

The biome range is the span of the four biome means. It is not a confidence interval,
and the biome intervals overlap heavily, EBF [1.00, 1.43] against DBF [1.21, 1.43].

### How much does the estimator matter?

The threshold is a zero crossing of a fitted curve, so the fit is not a detail. Script
`47` re-estimates it from the same data under 23 choices: polynomial degrees 2 to 6,
LOWESS at five bandwidths, smoothing splines over two orders of magnitude, four bin
widths and five fitting ranges.

All 23 fall between 0.155 and 0.247 sigma, which is 1.23 to 1.29 kPa, and the published
fourth-order polynomial sits at the median. For comparison, the biome differences span
1.22 to 1.32 kPa and the reported fit interval spans 1.16 to 1.36 kPa. The estimator
matters less than either.

Bin width barely registers, 0.008 sigma across a fivefold change. LOWESS runs
systematically lowest, 0.155 to 0.174, so the non-polynomial estimate sits slightly below
the polynomial rather than centred on it.

### Does any single site carry it?

Script `47` drops each of the 208 sites in turn, re-aggregates the remaining curves and
refits. The 208 thresholds run from 1.253 to 1.268 kPa with a median of 1.264, which is the
published value. The largest shift is 0.010 kPa, when US-CMW is dropped.

Table 1 shows that range rather than an interval. Any two of the 208 values share 207 sites,
so they are not independent draws, and a percentile over them would not mean what an interval
means. The per-site values are written to
`47_THRESHOLD_LeaveOneSiteOut_NEP_ZSCORE.csv`.

### Three points, not one

Script `81` separates quantities that a single "threshold" conflates. Across all sites
the VPD effect peaks at 0.47 kPa, crosses zero at 1.26 kPa and falls fastest at 1.50 kPa.
Only the zero crossing is the published threshold.

The script also flags any point landing within 2 % of the edge of the observed range. The
minimum does so in every group, because the fitted curve is still falling where the data
stop, so the effect does not bottom out within the observed VPD range.

### Do the biomes differ?

The intervals on Figure 4 come from the polynomial's prediction band on the aggregated
curve, so they describe how well the curve is pinned down, not how much sites differ.
Script `49` answers the other question by fitting one threshold per site and comparing
the distributions.

Kruskal-Wallis gives H = 12.17, p = 0.0068, so the four biomes are not one distribution.
Of the six pairs, only ENF against DBF and DBF against MF survive a Holm correction.
Every comparison involving EBF is indistinguishable.

Worth more than the tests: the range of biome medians is 0.189 sigma while the widest
within-biome IQR is 0.523 sigma. Sites within a biome differ nearly three times more than
the biomes differ from each other.

## ERA5 climate normals {#era5-climate-normals}

`17_add_era5_info.py` produces one 30-year (1991-2020) mean annual temperature and
precipitation per site from three possible sources: the ERA5 fields embedded in the
FLUXNET files, the Copernicus CDS API, and Google Earth Engine. Temperature and
precipitation always come from the same source for a given site, and the choice is
driven by precipitation.

Below 2000 mm per year, FLUXNET wins if it is available. Above that the value is
checked against the other two:

- Copernicus within 300 mm of FLUXNET: keep FLUXNET
- Copernicus higher than FLUXNET: keep FLUXNET
- Copernicus lower and further than 300 mm away: use Copernicus
- Copernicus exactly zero: reject it as a failed download, then compare Earth Engine
  against FLUXNET and take the lower of the two

Sites without FLUXNET ERA5 fall back to Copernicus if non-zero, otherwise Earth Engine.
Every decision, with the values behind it, is written to a timestamped log next to the
output.
